transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, hello Doctor. I came in today because... honestly, I just feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. It’s this constant feeling like I have to jump up and do the next thing, even when I am just completely worn out and really should be sitting still. 

But sitting still is... well, it reminds me of when my sister tried to make me sit through that awful play down at the community theater last month. The seats were so stiff, and she bought the tickets for my birthday, so I couldn't just get up and leave. We drove her Buick there, the one with the broken air conditioning. It was absolutely sweltering. She refuses to get it fixed because her mechanic retired in, oh, it must have been 2018. 

But anyway, even in my own house, in my comfortable chair, I just can't rest. I’m exhausted, but my body just wants to go. I don't even know how my sister sits through those long plays. Do you go to the theater much?
When you need to focus on something, do you often have trouble keeping your attention on it?

Well, yes, actually. I mean, I try to focus. I'll sit down with the senior center newsletter, or maybe the choir schedule—oh, I sing alto in the community choir, have for years. Our director, Mrs. Higgins, she’s a lovely woman, but she insists on these incredibly complicated arrangements. Last Christmas we did this piece that had us switching time signatures every other measure. It was exhausting. And her husband, bless his heart, he tries to help by handing out the sheet music, but he always gets the pages mixed up. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, focusing. So I'll sit down with the newsletter or the schedule, and I start out just fine. But then, after a few minutes, I realize my eyes have just been going over the same lines again and again, and I have absolutely no idea what I just read. It's like my brain just went on a little vacation without telling me. Have you ever been to Florida? My cousin went there last winter and said the humidity was just unbearable.
Did you have trouble paying attention like this as a child, before age 12?

Well, yes, actually. I mean, even back in grade school, it was always the same story. My mother saved all my report cards in this big cedar chest she kept at the foot of her bed. It smelled so strongly of mothballs, you know? She bought it at an estate sale from the Johnsons down the street when they moved to Ohio. Mr. Johnson had gotten a job at a tire factory, I think. Or maybe it was auto parts. 

But anyway, those report cards... the teachers always wrote the exact same things. They'd say I was bright, but careless. Always losing my spelling papers or talking out of turn. Mrs. Gable in third grade—she had this enormous beehive hairdo that never moved an inch, even in a stiff breeze—she was always having to remind me to stay in my seat or finish my arithmetic. I just couldn't seem to help it. Do you remember those old wooden desks with the inkwells? They were so fascinating to look at, much more interesting than long division.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, predominantly inattentive presentation: longstanding inattention since childhood with careless mistakes/losing papers, difficulty sustaining attention, and distractibility.
